agree.reason: Opening with a plain admission of the missed updates and then giving the bad news straight should win back a cold investor's trust, but there's no fundraising plan or ask tied to the next round, so they have nothing concrete to act on.

honest.reason: Every figure holds up against the brief (13% share, +$5,500 excluding the chain, just under 11 months, almost half of no-shows gone), though the claim that clinics like the chain had to switch schedulers to get reminders is an inference the brief doesn't state.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out runway, the lost account's share of revenue, $5,500 of underlying growth hidden by flat MRR, and the size of the no-show reduction, each in its most favourable true form, but it doesn't turn the $150 price into how many sales would matter.

right_comparison.reason: It gives flat revenue and 11 months of cash honestly, but never says what happens if nothing changes (cash runs out around next autumn) or what the standalone product must do to change that.

qualification.reason: 'The next few months will show whether that product sells' names an uncertain outcome and a reporting date, but gives no target number and no consequence if it is missed.

objections.reason: It meets the missed-updates complaint and the platform-risk worry directly, but leaves open the investor's obvious questions: when the company raises, and what happens if the reminder product doesn't sell.

fit.reason: It's a clear investor-update email of about 430 words, inside the 500-word limit, with a precise subject line and scannable sections.
